column3: Explicitly joins choosing false protectors with the mistaken belief that one is rightly guided.
The nearby resurrection scene supplies context, but it does not clarify misguided effort or self-deception.
God's awareness of wrongdoers corrects the false confidence implicit in their self-assessment.
Preferring worldly life over the hereafter is named as profound misguidance, explaining the focus's worldly loss.
The immediately preceding question introduces the people whose works are most lost.
Evil work made attractive and perceived as good is a direct parallel to the focus's false self-judgment.
Their mistaken assumption about God's knowledge concerns secrecy, not the evaluation of their efforts.
The nearby presentation of Hell gives the eschatological setting for the focus's judgment.
Noah's instruction and the drowning of wrongdoers do not clarify the focus's themes.
Contrasts the focus's lost worldly striving with believing effort directed toward the hereafter and accepted by God.
The immediate continuation identifies disbelief in God's signs and meeting Him as why their deeds are nullified.
The opening contrast of warning and reward for righteous works frames the standard missing from the focus's apparent good work.
Warns that wealth and children can be a means of punishment in worldly life rather than evidence of success.
The local description of eyes veiled from remembrance supplies the heedlessness behind the focus's mistaken work.
God's fulfilled promise and retribution are only a broad consequence parallel.
Sets stability of faith against the misguidance of wrongdoers across worldly life and the hereafter.
The garden owner's self-wronging certainty is a nearby example of deluded worldly judgment.
Lowering the gaze is a specific ethical command, only distantly related to distorted perception.
Worldly life is made attractive to disbelievers, furnishing a social contrast to their apparent success.
Its warning against taking protectors besides God leads directly into the focus's description of the disbelievers.
The Noah narrative repeats a divine instruction without bearing on self-deceived worldly effort.
Misleading outward appearance has a limited connection to mistaking appearances for true worth.
The garden owner's denial of the Hour and presumed better return dramatize false confidence in worldly fortune.
The narrative appearance of the sleepers is unrelated to moral self-deception.
Worldly life deceives those who ignored warning and meet God as disbelievers.
The local consequence of treating God's signs and messengers with mockery completes the focus's condemnation.
Reward for doers of good gives a bare contrast but does not distinguish real goodness from imagined goodness.
Reward for a good deed is a general outcome, already better specified by closer contrasts.
The immediate contrast promises Paradise to believers who do righteous deeds.
Failure to expect reckoning supports the focus's consequence but adds little to the diagnosis.
Affirms that every person's striving will be seen, opposing confidence in an unexamined effort.
Eternal contentment in Paradise continues the local positive outcome without clarifying the focus's error.
The enduring reward after faith and righteous deeds contrasts with lost worldly effort and its false appearance.
Outward spending and prayer are rejected when rooted in disbelief and unwillingness, a concrete warning about unaccepted deeds.
God's inexhaustible words are nearby context but do not interpret lost striving.
It reserves the best reward for those who truly do good, contrasting the focus's merely imagined goodness.
Satisfaction with one's striving in the final state contrasts with the worldly striver's mistaken satisfaction.
It gives the corrective criterion: hope for meeting God, righteous work, and worship without association.
The question about the cave companions is a narrative transition without a close thematic link.
A mistaken battlefield assessment is a different use of supposition.
The parable of worldly life as transient vegetation exposes the setting in which the focus's effort is lost.
Obedience to God and the Messenger brings companionship with the righteous, providing a positive path for rightly directed action.
Mistaking moving mountains for still ones is physical perception, not moral self-evaluation.
God's religion and worship are a general positive contrast with little additional explanation.
States that such people are the losers in the hereafter, reinforcing the focus's ultimate loss.
The description of good and beautiful companions has no material relation to the focus.
The prohibition regarding hypocrites' funerals concerns their disbelief but not their deluded work.
Abraham's model of dissociation from false worship supplies a contrary allegiance to the focus's misguided orientation.
Distinguishes those astray from the guided under divine knowledge, supporting the focus's contrast between appearance and true direction.
Its exemplary model and hope in God are broad positive guidance only.
The statement that most earlier peoples went astray is too general to clarify the focus.
The believers' trial before entering Paradise concerns endurance, not illusory goodness.
The scale of recompense for good and evil deeds adds only a general accountability frame.
The contrast of two outcomes in conflict does not address the focus's self-deceived striving.
The Prophet is explicitly not astray, forming a concise contrary image to the focus's lost strivers.
God's judgment is best, challenging the human standard by which the focus's people count their work good.
Treating God's enemies as allies is named as departure from the straight way, a specific misguided action.
Replacing wrong with good after wrongdoing is a repentance promise, not the focus's false evaluation.
The covenant's conditions and deviation after disbelief provide only a broad guidance contrast.
Forgetting what was recalled to them leads to division and later accounting, clarifying heedless deviation.
The destruction of Pharaoh's constructions after patient believers inherit shows worldly accomplishment overturned by divine judgment.
They are turned from the path while thinking themselves guided, closely matching the focus's deluded condition.
One who comes earnestly striving is too fragmentary to illuminate the focus's lost striving.
Returning disputed matters to God and the Messenger supplies an authoritative corrective to self-certified goodness.
Building as though one will live forever has a limited worldly-illusion connection.
God's beautiful names do not clarify the focus's judgment of deeds.
Moses's staff becoming a serpent is unrelated to the focus.
Those who mistake the restrained poor for rich offer a limited but concrete parallel of deceptive appearance, with a social corrective.
God's selection of Moses does not bear on lost worldly work.
Denial of purposeless creation and return to God confronts the absent final accountability behind the focus's error.
Those seeking worldly life and its adornment receive their deeds there, sharply contrasting the lasting value presumed by the focus.
The threatened ruin of the garden continues the nearby worldly-wealth parable but is already sufficiently represented.
Explicitly states that some deeds are nullified in this world and the hereafter, closely explaining lost effort.
A person's false assumption of invulnerability is a distant form of self-deception.
Abraham's worldly and final goodness is a general positive contrast.
The hypocrites' reaction to another's fortune does not clarify the focus.
The division and testing of Israel contains only a broad distinction between righteous and otherwise.
Denial of bodily resurrection supplies a limited accountability contrast.
Knowing only the outward side of worldly life while heedless of the hereafter closely diagnoses the focus's misplaced effort.
Questions whether wealth and children are mistaken as signs of favor, challenging worldly measures of success.
Disbelief in the hereafter leads to deeds being made attractive so that people wander blindly.
General recompense for good and evil actions adds little after closer accounting verses.
Extended worldly advantage is not good for disbelievers but an increase in sin, correcting false success.
The queen's initial visual mistake and later submission provide only an indirect contrast.
Trading the hereafter for worldly life gives a direct account of the inverted valuation underlying lost worldly striving.
Leaving those who distort God's names is a specific prohibition with little link to the focus's work theme.
Core traits of the God-conscious are a broad positive contrast only.
Affirming the best is too brief to add interpretive clarity.
Treating religion as play and being deceived by worldly life leads to forgetting the final meeting.
The excellence of an eternal abode is too general to add to the focus.
The contrast between seeking worldly gain and the hereafter in a moment of disobedience gives a contextual instance of divided aims.
Rejecting truth and lying about God lead to Hell, a broad consequence without the focus's self-deception.
Its account of the Fire's guardians and testing does not clarify lost effort.
Moses's request for Aaron's assistance is unrelated.
The repeated reward formula does not distinguish true good from imagined good.
Following Pharaoh's unsound command offers a concrete example of following a path that is not rightly directed.
The account of souls in death and sleep has no close connection.
Others' wish to turn believers back to disbelief is a distant deviation parallel.
Entering among God's servants gives a very general contrary outcome.
Fruit, intoxicant, and provision do not clarify the focus's themes.
Those who claim to be reformers while causing corruption directly parallel the focus's self-deceived claim to good work.
It explicitly reverses their self-description: they are corrupters but do not perceive it.
Their attempt to deceive God and believers in fact deceives only themselves, though they do not realize it.
Seeking a way other than submission to God is rejected and ends in loss in the hereafter.
Those pleased with what they have done and seeking praise for what they did not do expose another false assessment of moral worth.
Disbelief nullifies deeds and leaves a person among the losers in the hereafter.
Association with God would render even the prophets' deeds void, establishing the decisive standard beyond apparent work.
Following conjecture and surmise instead of divine guidance explains how a person can go astray while feeling assured.
Denying God's signs and the final meeting makes deeds worthless, closely matching the local explanation in 18:105.
Those who deny faith cannot maintain God's places of worship; their deeds have become worthless.
Enjoying one's worldly share like earlier peoples ends with works becoming fruitless in this world and the next.
Those content with worldly life, at rest in it, and heedless of God's signs provide a direct profile of misplaced worldly orientation.
The immediate sequel to 11:15 says their worldly construction is void and their works are futile in the hereafter.
Worldly provision is expanded and restricted, yet worldly life is only a brief enjoyment beside the hereafter.
Their hearts, hearing, and sight are sealed, and they are the heedless, clarifying the blindness of their judgment.
Whoever seeks the immediate world may receive it, but is then assigned to Hell, sharply contrasting worldly effort with ultimate success.
Blindness in this world carries into the hereafter, extending the focus's imagery of distorted perception.
Earthly adornment is a test of who is best in deed, distinguishing true excellence from merely worldly production.
The adornment of earth will be reduced to barren ground, exposing the transience of the focus's worldly arena.
Do not turn one's eyes from devoted believers seeking worldly adornment; this is a direct local corrective to worldly valuation.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and hope.
Turning away from God's signs and forgetting one's prior deeds describes culpable heedlessness and self-destruction.
Later generations neglected prayer and followed desires, giving a concrete path from devotion's loss to ruin.
Turning away from divine remembrance brings a constricted life and resurrection in blindness, the inverse of true guidance.
Do not extend the eyes toward worldly splendor given to others; the Lord's provision is better and more lasting.
Conditional worship that is satisfied only by worldly good shows a faith judged by immediate outcome rather than truth.
The deeds of disbelievers are like a mirage: apparent substance vanishes on arrival before God and His reckoning.
God renders the deeds they performed into scattered dust, an explicit image of lost effort.
Worldly life is diversion and play, while the true life belongs to the final abode.
Buying distracting discourse to lead people from God's path without knowledge is an active form of misguided worldly action.
Neither worldly life nor the Deceiver should be allowed to mislead regarding God.
Wealth and children are falsely claimed as proof of divine favor and immunity from punishment.
Wealth and children do not bring people near to God; only faith and righteous work do.
Worldly life and the Deceiver are both named as sources of deception concerning God.
Association with God would make deeds worthless and leave the person among the losers.
Seeking the harvest of this world yields only a worldly portion and no share in the hereafter.
Worldly houses and furnishings are allotted to those who disbelieve, showing that material abundance is not a measure of rightness.
All worldly ornament is only enjoyment of this life; the hereafter with God is for the God-conscious.
Taking God's signs in mockery and being deceived by worldly life leads to the Fire, uniting the focus's central motifs.
Disbelief and hindering God's path cause deeds to be lost.
Hating what God revealed leads God to render their deeds worthless.
One who turns from remembrance and wants only worldly life is to be turned away from, directly naming the focus's orientation.
Worldly life is play, diversion, adornment, boasting, and competition in wealth and children before it fades away.
Satan makes his party forget God's remembrance, explaining a route to heedless misdirection.
Wealth and children must not distract from God's remembrance; those distracted are the losers.
Wealth and children are a test, correcting their use as a measure of success.
Transgression and preference for worldly life explicitly identify the choice underlying final ruin.
Hell is the refuge for the one who preferred worldly life.
Fearing one's standing before God and restraining desire gives the contrary discipline to worldly misdirection.
Paradise is the refuge for the one who restrains desire in view of final accountability.
The preference for worldly life is directly condemned.
The hereafter is declared better and more enduring than worldly life.
